data_section_full_text:
5 Data


Our sample period covers the first fiscal quarter of 2005 to the third fiscal quarter of
2010. We collect bond issues and rating histories from the Fixed Income Securities
Database (FISD). Following prior literature, we exclude bonds that are unusual
(exchangeable, convertible, putable, asset-backed, enhanced, or preferred) or junior.
We require issues to receive ratings from at least two of Moody’s, Standard &
Poor’s, and Fitch; few (1–3 %) firms receive ratings from only one of these
agencies. We exclude firms in default (i.e., with D-rated bonds). Our main sample
comprises 3,437 bonds issued by 711 firms and 44,148 bond-quarter observations.
We match bond issues with bond issuers in Moody’s Financial Metrics database and
collect the issuers’ reported financial statement data from that database. We classify
123

Financial statement comparability and credit risk


issuers into peer groups using Moody’s industry classifications. We obtain data on
firms’ auditors and audit fees from Audit Analytics. We obtain data on firms’
segments and alternative industry classifications from Compustat. We obtain stock
return data from CRSP.

We discuss the calculation and interpretation of the comparability measures in
Sect. 2. Table 1 provides descriptive statistics for these measures and the other
model variables. The average median adjustment to interest coverage reduces the
ratio by 0.83, because Moody’s almost always reclassifies off-balance sheet
financing as on-balance sheet, not the reverse. There is substantial variation in the
median adjustment to coverage across peer group-quarter observations (‘‘peerquarters’’): from -0.89 for the 25th percentile to -0.22 for the 75th percentile. The
interquartile range for the adjustment to coverage (i.e., minus iqr_cover_delta)
averages -2.77 and ranges from -0.70 for the 25th percentile to -3.23 for the 75th
percentile across peer-quarters.

For most observations, the adjustment for non-recurring items is a positive but
fairly small percentage of revenues, the largest number on the income statement,
because credit analysts are more likely to reclassify ‘‘recurring’’ gains as non-recurring
and ‘‘non-recurring’’ losses as recurring than the opposite cases. The interquartile
range for the adjustment to coverage (i.e., minus iqr_nonrecurr_delta_sRev) averages
-0.02 across peer-quarters.

There is substantial variation across peer-quarters in the level and variability of
economic fundamentals within peer-quarters. The average bond in the sample has a
face value of $393,319, 3,481 days till maturity, and average_rating_bond equal to
9.40, which corresponds to a BBB rating. The average of bsmprob, i.e., the annual
market-implied default probability, is 1.5 %.

We use TRACE (Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine) transactions for
traded corporate bonds to estimate Roll’s (1984) measure of bid-ask spreads
described in Sect. 4 and Eq. (1) and also credit spreads for those bonds. We clean
the TRACE data to eliminate reporting errors following methodology in DickNielsen (2009).

To mitigate the effects of outliers, we measure roll first on rolling windows of 21
days during each quarter, using only days with at least one transaction and requiring
at least four transactions in each window. We then take the median of these
measures within the quarter. The percentiles of roll for our sample are very similar
to those reported in Dick-Nielsen et al. (2012).

We calculate bond yields as the average yields for all trades on dates that the
issuer files quarterly financial statements. If a bond does not trade on a filing date,
we use the first yield available following the filing date. We calculate bond spreads
(bond_spread) as the difference between the bond yield and the interpolated
maturity-matched Treasury yield on the same day as the yield is measured.
